How Xcode builds your Kotlin

Puzzle 26 left your frameworks in Gradle's build folder. But the iOS developer presses Run in Xcode, and Xcode knows nothing about Gradle. Here's the one script that makes every Xcode build start Gradle first, the task it runs, and where the framework goes.

  • Puzzle 24: "One binary: the linker"

    LLVM writes object code, instructions in which each call still names its target by a symbol. The linker, the last step of the link stage, joins object code into one binary and connects each call to the address its symbol names. In a release build, dead code elimination has already dropped unreached code from the IR, before LLVM, and the linker trims a little more; an exported module can't be trimmed, because Swift, outside this build, might call any of it.

The problem

Puzzle 26 left your frameworks under Gradle's build folder: build/bin/iosArm64/debugFramework/shared.framework and the rest. The iOS developer doesn't open a terminal. They press Run in Xcode, for the simulator, after you changed a function in commonMain. Xcode compiles Swift; it has never heard of Gradle. So who runs Gradle, which of the link tasks from puzzle 23 does it run, and how does the new framework end up where Swift's import shared finds it, and inside the app, as puzzle 25 said a dynamic framework must be?

See it

The building block

Xcode builds an app target as an ordered list of steps, its build phases. You see them in the target's Build Phases tab: Compile Sources compiles the Swift files, Link Binary With Libraries runs the linker, and so on, top to bottom.

One kind of build phase runs whatever you tell it: a Run Script phase, a shell script that Xcode runs at its place in the list, every build. That's the bridge to Gradle. Kotlin's docs give the script to paste into a new Run Script phase:

if [ "YES" = "$OVERRIDE_KOTLIN_BUILD_IDE_SUPPORTED" ]; then
  echo "Skipping Gradle build task invocation due to OVERRIDE_KOTLIN_BUILD_IDE_SUPPORTED environment variable set to \"YES\""
  exit 0
fi
cd "$SRCROOT/.."
./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode

$SRCROOT is the iOS project's folder, so cd "$SRCROOT/.." steps up to the root of your Gradle project, and :shared is your shared module's name. The first four lines are a guard: when you start the iOS app from Android Studio instead, the IDE has already built the framework and sets that variable, so the script skips a second build.

The task, embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode, comes from the multiplatform plugin, and it exists only if your iOS targets declare binaries.framework. It reads what Xcode is building right now (the simulator or a real iPhone, Debug or Release) and then:

  1. runs the one link task for that platform and configuration, such as linkDebugFrameworkIosSimulatorArm64: not every target, and never the XCFramework;
  2. copies the new framework into Xcode's derived data: the folder where Xcode keeps its own build output for this project, next to the app it's building;
  3. embeds and signs it, puzzle 25's Embed & Sign, done for you.

Because the framework lands in Xcode's own build output, Swift's import shared finds it without a search path you'd have to set by hand.

Three settings from Kotlin's docs make this reliable, and each has a reason:

  • Move the Run Script phase above Compile Sources. Swift is compiled against the framework's header (puzzle 5), so the framework must exist first.
  • Untick "Based on dependency analysis". The script lists no input or output files, so Xcode can't tell whether your Kotlin changed; unticking makes it run the script on every build, on purpose, without warning about missing outputs each time.
  • Turn off User Script Sandboxing in Build Settings. With it on, Xcode lets a script touch only the files listed as its inputs, and Gradle reads your whole project.

A custom build configuration, other than Debug or Release, needs one more setting, KOTLIN_FRAMEWORK_BUILD_TYPE, set to Debug or Release, so the task knows which kind of framework to link. Other ways of handing a framework to an iOS team that doesn't build Kotlin itself are module 7's (coming soon).

The analogy

The restaurant from puzzle 25 has a fixed opening routine, a checklist the head chef runs top to bottom. You add one line near the top: "phone the print shop". The print shop prints only today's edition, for today's kind of service, and delivers it to the kitchen's own shelf, already stamped. By the time the cooks start (Compile Sources), the cookbook is where they always look.

Check yourself

On a fresh checkout, the Run Script phase sits below Compile Sources. The developer presses Run. What happens?

Not quite. Build phases run in the listed order, top to bottom; the script would come after Compile Sources.

Right. The framework must exist before Swift is compiled.

Not quite. The task links only one framework; the problem is order: Swift compiles before it exists.

Why does pressing Run in Xcode link one Kotlin framework, not the whole XCFramework from puzzle 26?

Not quite. Xcode reads XCFrameworks fine (puzzle 26); this task builds only what this build needs.

Right. One build, one framework.

Not quite. Nothing is remembered: the task never asks for the other targets.

Your Kotlin framework is dynamic, the default, and you set it up with this Run Script. What puts it inside the app, so dyld finds it at launch?

Not quite. The script doesn't change the kind; a Kotlin framework is dynamic unless isStatic is set (puzzle 25).

Not quite. dyld only loads files that are inside the app on the phone; something must embed the framework first.

Right. The task embeds and signs for you.

What you now know

Xcode builds an app as an ordered list of build phases. A Run Script phase placed before Compile Sources runs ./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode, which links the one framework for the platform and configuration Xcode is building, then copies it into Xcode's own build output and signs it. So Swift finds the framework without any path set by hand, and a dynamic framework is embedded for you.
